node.label: Susan G. Pedersen
node.date_label: Family, Dependence (1993) · Eleanor Rathbone (2004) · Settler Colonialism, coedited (2005) · The Guardians (2015)
node.description: In Family, Dependence, and the Origins of the Welfare State (1993), Susan Pedersen argues that welfare policies in Britain and France were shaped by gender relations and support for dependent family members as well as class politics, with different consequences for wages and citizenship. In The Guardians (2015), she argues that the League of Nations mandates system changed imperial sovereignty by subjecting colonial rule to international scrutiny and petitioning, helping make statehood possible without simply improving colonial government. Her work connects comparative welfare history, feminism and the history of international institutions. Eleanor Rathbone and the Politics of Conscience (2004) places feminist social reform within parliamentary and imperial politics; the collection coedited with Caroline Elkins (2005) treats settler colonialism comparatively. The Guardians won the Cundill Prize in 2015.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Family, Dependence, and the Origins of the Welfare State: Britain and France, 1914–1945 (1993); After the Victorians: Private Conscience and Public Duty in Modern Britain (1994), coedited with Peter Mandler; Eleanor Rathbone and the Politics of Conscience (2004); Settler Colonialism in the Twentieth Century: Projects, Practices, Legacies (2005), coedited with Caroline Elkins; Back to the League of Nations (2007); The Guardians: The League of Nations and the Crisis of Empire (2015).
node.scope_note: Family, Dependence, Eleanor Rathbone and The Guardians were not read in full: argument claims use identified institutional/publisher summaries and Goebel’s review. The 2005 introduction was read only in selected licensed-preview passages. Selected passages of Pedersen’s 2019 review and the complete 2025 coauthored interlude were read; their subjects’ books were not independently read. Earlier articles were identified bibliographically, not read as argument evidence.

proposed_edges.relationship: Mazower’s 2015 review credits The Guardians (2015) with transforming understanding of the League of Nations.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Review, paragraphs beginning Susan Pedersen’s and Now Pedersen; “strikingly original”. Book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In I want to love it (2019), Pedersen argues that the marginalization of women, Africa and culture in Hobsbawm’s historical synthesis follows from its organizing assumptions.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Final analytical paragraph beginning At the end of his book: “constitutive, not lapses”. She also praises his explanatory reach. Hobsbawm’s books unread here.

proposed_edges.relationship: In I want to love it (2019), Pedersen values Evans’s Eric Hobsbawm: A Life in History (2019) but questions its individual focus when explaining his institutional and publishing success.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Paragraph beginning I am not criticising Hobsbawm: “isn’t really the right medium”; opening assessment praises the biography. Evans’s book unread here.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Settler Colonialism: A Concept and Its Uses (2005), Elkins and Pedersen use Wolfe’s structural account while distinguishing their twentieth-century cases.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction p. 3: “Wolfe alerts us”; pp. 3–4 distinguish cases. Joint attribution retained; Wolfe’s book unread.
proposed_edges.map_label: Uses and differentiates Wolfe’s structural account

proposed_edges.relationship: The Guardians (2015) explains how international scrutiny and petitioning within the mandates system reshaped imperial sovereignty and the possibilities of statehood.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Re-based at Claude verification (2026-11-01). OUP abstract supports the claim on its own (online 18 June 2015). The second cited source (Goebel, H-Soz-Kult) was not accessible to me: the site served an Anubis bot check, the H-Net mirror returned 403 and the Wayback copy was bot-blocked. The coordinator may drop sp_w_goebel_review from this edge's source_ids. Phrase seen: “placed imperial rule under intense public scrutiny; exploited new rights of petition; brought normative statehood nearer but changed its nature; mattered not because it altered governance” Read at: https://academic.oup.com/book/6410

proposed_edges.relationship: With Elkins, Pedersen’s Settler Colonialism: A Concept and Its Uses (2005) proposes a comparative typology of settler power and privilege.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction pp. 1–4 and 17–18: “definition” and “typology”. Selected preview passages read; later chapters unread. Joint credit retained.

proposed_edges.relationship: In Family, Dependence, and the Origins of the Welfare State (1993), Susan Pedersen contributed to comparative social history by reconstructing the competing interests and processes that produced different welfare policies in Britain and France, as Maria Sophia Quine emphasizes in her 1999 review.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the complete review on pp. 149–150 in the publisher-hosted review section. Quine situates the book within empirically grounded social histories of welfare and identifies policy formation as its distinctive contribution. She also criticizes its limited attention to lived effects and its rationalistic account of reformers. The book itself was not read; this edge records the review’s assessment, not a claim that it founded a school.
proposed_edges.map_label: Comparative social history of welfare policy formation

proposed_edges.relationship: Susan Pedersen’s 2010 round-table review of Ross McKibbin’s Parties and People (2010) contributed to debate on interwar British political culture by stressing the electoral importance of international credibility and the Conservatives’ liberal-imperialist self-presentation, an argument Helen McCarthy uses in “Whose Democracy?” (2012).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read McCarthy’s substantive discussion and footnote 24 on Cambridge Core. The body expressly adopts Pedersen’s point to question the electoral marginality of foreign affairs. Pedersen’s original review was not read. This records a specific intervention received in political historiography; it is not an edge for participation in a round-table or for collective credit.
proposed_edges.map_label: International affairs in interwar electoral politics
